description: We are a team of Computer Science students passionate about AI, Machine Learning, Data Science, and Software Engineering. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we're tackling Flame in Freefall, aiming to make microgravity combustion research more accessible through AI-powered analysis and visualization. We welcome teammates skilled in AI/ML, Python, Data Engineering,  or Physics. We value innovation, collaboration, and solving real-world challenges.
summary:
OrbitFlame is a project developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the "Flame in Freefall" challenge.

Our project explores how combustion behaves in microgravity and how reduced gravity affects flame characteristics compared with conditions on Earth.

By making space-based combustion research more accessible and understandable, OrbitFlame aims to help students, researchers, and space enthusiasts explore the scientific importance of studying flames in microgravity.

The project highlights the relevance of combustion research to spacecraft fire safety and our understanding of physical processes in space.
details:
OrbitFlame is an interactive research dashboard that helps researchers, engineers, and students discover, compare, and understand NASA’s microgravity combustion investigations. It addresses a central challenge: turning complex, scattered experimental information into clear, traceable insights relevant to spacecraft fire safety.

Users can explore investigations by research topic and fuel family, understand why a study is relevant, and compare two or three investigations side by side. Comparisons distinguish research objectives, experimental variables, described measurements, available dataset fields, and interpretation limits.

The prototype includes four curated investigations—FLEX, BASS, BASS-II, and SPICE—and document retrieval over 81 passages from three NASA reports. Retrieved evidence includes links to original PDF pages. A measurement explorer displays 12 reviewed FLEX records, preserving units and missing values.

OrbitFlame uses Flutter and Dart for the web interface, ASP.NET Core and C# for the backend, and Python with Poppler for offline document processing and source checks. BM25 retrieves relevant passages. A configurable language-model adapter supports retrieval-augmented generation, with response-format and citation-ID validation. Without a configured model, the dashboard provides clearly labeled source excerpts and curated comparison summaries.

The project’s creative contribution is connecting study discovery, comparison, document evidence, and numerical exploration within one research workflow. Its intended impact is to reduce the effort required to identify useful evidence and understand its applicability to fire prevention, detection, and suppression.

We considered scientific traceability, differences between experimental conditions, incomplete data, measurement definitions, and the distinction between observed findings and generated interpretation. Future development includes hybrid retrieval, broader study coverage, and scenario-based evidence assessment. The current prototype supports research interpretation rather than validated predictions of new fire scenarios.
